column1: # ZAP baseline alerts we have decided about. Everything else fails the build.
# Tab-separated: <rule id>
# IGNORE is a decision, not a mute button. Every line here has to say why the
# alert is not worth acting on, or which issue is acting on it — an entry that
# says neither is how a scan turns into a formality. The rule ids are ZAP's:
# https://www.zaproxy.org/docs/alerts/
# Also read: apps/api/src/http/security-headers.ts and
# apps/web/src/lib/security-headers.ts, which are why this file is as short as it
# is. Four of the eleven alerts in the first run were fixed rather than listed —
# nosniff on /favicon.svg and /robots.txt, a Permissions-Policy on the built
# assets, CORP and COOP everywhere, and a year of caching on the hashed bundles
# that were being revalidated on every navigation. The alternative to fixing an
# alert is not always ignoring it.
# Note that zap-baseline counts an INFORMATIONAL alert as a WARN unless it is
# listed here, so two of the lines below are about noise rather than risk. That
# is worth knowing before reading the length of this file as a measure of debt.
# An entry that has stopped firing is deleted, not left to be believed — the same
# rule scripts/audit-gate.mjs enforces for advisories. `10109` (Modern Web
# Application) was here until the scan gained a session and a browser spider:
# ZAP stopped observing that it could not crawl a JavaScript app, because it
# now can. `10038` (CSP header not set) was here until #134 sent one: the
# dashboard's documents now carry a policy with a per-response nonce, so the
# alert it stood for no longer exists and the line went with it.

column3: One rule id for three headers. CORP and COOP ARE sent, on every response, and are asserted by unit tests in both apps — this covers only Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy, which is deliberately absent: require-corp buys cross-origin isolation (SharedArrayBuffer, precise timers) that this app does not want, and costs every cross-origin subresource having to opt in, so the first external avatar or font anyone adds would break silently.

/reset-password?token. A reset token in a URL is how an emailed reset link works — every implementation of one. It is single-use, expires, and Referrer-Policy keeps the path off cross-origin requests. Removing it means moving to a code the user retypes, which is a product decision and not a header.

Private IP Disclosure on /assets/index-*.js. The match is the literal "10.0.0.0/8" inside the TRUST_PROXY validation message in apps/web/src/lib/env.ts, which is documentation of the expected format, not an address of any deployment. Verified in the built bundle.

Storable/Non-Storable Content. This one fires BECAUSE the headers are right: it reports every no-store response as "non-storable" and every hashed asset as "cacheable", which is the split apps/web/src/lib/security-headers.ts and the routeRules in vite.config.ts exist to produce. It is an observation, not a finding — zap-baseline counts informational alerts as WARN unless they are listed here. Both halves are asserted by unit tests and were verified against the running built server.

Information in Browser sessionStorage, on every authenticated page — the one alert the logged-in scan added. Looked at rather than assumed: no code of ours touches sessionStorage (`grep -rn sessionStorage apps/web/src` is empty), and the only write in the built bundle is TanStack Router's reload guard, keyed `tanstack_router_reload:<error message>`, which exists to stop a reload loop when a chunk fails to load. An asset-load error message, not a tenant's data. Listed rather than left off because it fires on every run and zap-baseline's accounting of informational alerts has already changed once.
